blocks.text: 1. Metadata Filtering

blocks.alt: A query goes through vector search and a metadata filter to produce narrowed results

blocks.text: Collections set a hard structural boundary. Metadata Filtering gives that promised softer boundary its own full treatment, narrowing results within a single collection.
It combines vector similarity search with exact filters on structured fields.
2. Soft Boundaries Inside A Collection
A collection already sets a hard boundary; metadata filtering narrows further within it.
This gives a query fine grained control without requiring a separate collection for every case.
3. What Metadata Looks Like Here
As with metadata extraction in Document Ingestion, author, date, category, and source all travel alongside the vector.
Those same fields become filterable conditions at search time.
4. Pre-Filter Versus Post-Filter

blocks.alt: Pre-filter filters first while post-filter searches first

blocks.text: Pre filtering narrows candidates before similarity search runs; post filtering runs the filter after.
Those two orderings can produce meaningfully different results and performance.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Filtering order","Behavior"],"rows":[["Pre-filter","Narrows candidates before similarity comparison runs"],["Post-filter","Runs similarity comparison first, then filters the results"]]}

blocks.text: 5. The Empty Results Problem

blocks.alt: An overly strict filter returns no results

blocks.text: Post filtering can discard the top similarity matches, leaving too few or zero results left.
A narrow filter applied too late can silently starve a search of results.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Retrieving the top ten similarity matches and then post filtering by a narrow category can leave zero results if none of those top ten happened to match that category, even though better matches existed further down.

blocks.text: 6. Combining Multiple Conditions

blocks.alt: A category condition ANDs with a date condition

blocks.text: Real filters often combine several conditions together, like date range and category at once.
Most vector databases support combining these conditions with logical and or or logic.
7. Filter Performance Cost

blocks.alt: A simple filter is compared against a complex filter

blocks.text: As with what an index actually does in Indexing, filtering can bypass the speed benefits an index normally provides.
Some vector databases build specialized indexes that support filtering efficiently.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Filtering approach","Performance implication"],"rows":[["Naive filtering after search","Can bypass index speed benefits entirely"],["Filter aware indexing","Preserves much of the index's speed advantage"]]}

blocks.text: 8. Filtering As An Access Control Mechanism

blocks.alt: User permissions go through a metadata filter to produce allowed results only

blocks.text: As with multi tenant isolation in Collections, metadata filtering can enforce which chunks a specific user is allowed to see.
This combines retrieval relevance with permission enforcement in one single query.
9. Recognizing When Metadata Filtering Is The Right Tool

blocks.alt: Needing to narrow within a collection points toward metadata filtering

blocks.text: Narrowing results within one collection by attributes suits metadata filtering well.
Hard, permanent separation between datasets favors separate collections instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates pre-filtering candidates by metadata before ranking by similarity.

code.content:
documents = [
    {"id": "d1", "text": "Refund policy overview.", "category": "billing", "score": 0.92},
    {"id": "d2", "text": "Shipping timeline details.", "category": "logistics", "score": 0.88},
    {"id": "d3", "text": "Refund exceptions for damaged items.", "category": "billing", "score": 0.75},
]

def pre_filter_then_rank(documents, category_filter):
    # pre-filter versus post-filter
    candidates = [d for d in documents if d["category"] == category_filter]
    return sorted(candidates, key=lambda d: -d["score"])

def post_filter_after_rank(documents, category_filter, top_k):
    # the empty results problem
    ranked = sorted(documents, key=lambda d: -d["score"])[:top_k]
    return [d for d in ranked if d["category"] == category_filter]

pre_filtered = pre_filter_then_rank(documents, "billing")
print("Pre-filtered by category=billing, then ranked:")
for d in pre_filtered:
    print(f" {d}")

post_filtered = post_filter_after_rank(documents, "billing", top_k=1)
print(f"\nPost-filtered after taking only top 1 by score first (the empty results problem):")
print(f" results: {post_filtered}")
print(" Notice post-filtering with a small top_k can lose valid results.")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows pre-filtering returning both relevant billing documents, while post-filtering with a small top_k misses one of them entirely.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Post filtering with a small top_k, silently discarding valid results that never made the initial cut.
Applying complex, unindexed filters that bypass the speed benefits of a well built index.
Forgetting that metadata filtering can double as an access control mechanism for permissions.
Combining conditions incorrectly, mixing up intended and or or logic across multiple filters.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Metadata filtering combines vector similarity search with exact filters on structured fields.
A collection sets a hard boundary; metadata filtering narrows further within it as a softer boundary.
The same metadata fields captured during ingestion become filterable conditions at search time.
Pre-filtering narrows candidates before similarity search; post-filtering filters after ranking.
Post-filtering can discard top matches, leaving too few or zero results if applied too late.
Real filters often combine multiple conditions together using logical and or or logic.
Filtering can bypass an index's speed benefits unless the database supports filter aware indexing.
Metadata filtering can enforce access control, ensuring users only see permitted chunks.
